summary: Americans’ feelings toward China have warmed since 2021, though views remain mostly cold, with sharp partisan and generational divides.

title: Prediction markets’ trading volume doubled between May and July, largely driven by sports
summary: Prediction market trading on Kalshi and Polymarket doubled from May to July, mostly due to a large uptick in sports trading.

title: Americans’ views of data centers have turned more negative
summary: Americans’ views of data centers have turned more negative since January. But many are unsure or unfamiliar with them.

title: Tradition and Change Among Latter-day Saints in the U.S.
summary: Members of the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints are still highly religious and conservative, but signs point to demographic and social change.

title: Lifelong Latter-day Saints are more religious than both former members and converts
summary: The demographics of those who were raised in the church – and remain in it – also differ in notable ways from those who left or converted to it.

title: Latter-day Saints are highly religious, though not uniformly so
summary:
Latter-day Saints in the US are highly religious, though not uniformly so
Excerpt: Members of the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints living in the Mountain region and members who have more education are especially religious.

title: Latter-day Saints largely identify as Republican but stand out from their partisan peers on diversity issues
summary: Three-quarters of Latter-day Saint Republicans say racial and ethnic diversity strengthens the country, compared with six-in-ten Republicans overall.

title: Latter-day Saints: Happy in their family lives, traditional in gender roles
summary: Latter-day Saints are more likely than many other Americans to rate their family lives highly and to marry someone of the same religion.

title: Latter-day Saints have strong communal ties and high social trust
summary: About half of Latter-day Saints (48%) say most people can be trusted, compared with 34% of U.S. adults overall.

title: Do people trust China, the U.S. or the EU to regulate AI?
summary: Trust in China, the U.S. and the EU to regulate AI is tied to overall favorability. Many people trust their own country more than any other regulator.

title: Appendix: Detailed tables
Concerns about AI are especially widespread in high-income countries
summary: People in high-income countries are more likely than those in less wealthy nations to be concerned about AI, as well as its impact on jobs and economic inequality.

title: Who has heard or read a lot about AI, and how is awareness changing?
summary: Majorities in most of 37 countries surveyed have at least some awareness of AI. In some places, the share who has heard a lot about it has increased since last year.

title: What do young people around the world think about AI?
summary: A 37-country survey finds that young adults are particularly worried about AI leading to fewer jobs. Still, they're more likely than older people to feel both excited and concerned about AI.

title: Globally, More People Expect AI to Cause Job Loss Than Growth
summary: Amid a mix of concern and excitement about AI, a 37-country survey finds pessimism about its potential impact on jobs and economic inequality.

title: Democrats are now more worried than Republicans about AI and its impact on jobs
summary: In another shift, Democrats are now more likely than Republicans to predict that AI will lead to fewer jobs over the next 20 years (75% vs. 68%).
